# Repositioning Strategy — internal codename "Older Than the Noise"

**Version 5. Continues and completes Version 4 from §3.1. Sections 1 and 2 stand unchanged and are not restated; this document picks up the positioning statement mid-sentence and runs to the annexes.**

**Same convention on numbers.** Percentages of net revenue, of gross sales, or basis points of a named cost base. Absolute figures are left for the functions who own them to insert. Annex B carries the assumption register; each line has a name against it, and the name is an invitation, not an allocation of blame.

**A word on how this is written, since it has been raised.** Several sections below stop short of instructing. That is deliberate. Where a function owns the evidence, the document asks the question and leaves the answer to them; where the answer is genuinely ours to make, it is stated flatly. Readers who prefer directives throughout will find §9 and §13 sufficiently blunt. Readers who notice which passages were left open may draw their own conclusions about where the real uncertainty sits.

---

## 3. The positioning

### 3.1 Core idea: **the standard we never lowered**

> In a market where almost everything has been quietly made worse, this is the brand that was never cheapened.

*(Subject to Gate 0 — §2. Final wording follows the record, not the writing.)*

**Positioning statement, internal use, consumables branch:**

> For people who have noticed that their favourite things keep getting quietly worse, **[Brand]** is the everyday [category] that has not changed what matters in seventy years — because we publish what is in it, what has ever changed, and what we have committed never to change. Unlike own-label and dupe alternatives, whose specification is re-tendered whenever the commodity cycle moves, our standard is a published, verifiable commitment rather than a claim.

**The strategic sentence, if only one survives the deck:** *heritage plus ubiquity — the everyday thing that never got worse.* Nobody else in the set can hold both halves. Premium heritage brands have the first and not the second. Own label has the second and structurally cannot have the first.

### 3.2 Why this reaches two audiences with one idea

The temptation is to build a message for the base and a message for the recruit. That is what produced two campaigns and one apology. One idea, read differently, is the safer architecture — and the more interesting one.

| | What the base hears | What the provenance-led under-35 hears |
|---|---|---|
| The claim | "They didn't sell us out." Vindication of a forty-year purchase habit | "This is checkable." An unusual invitation to verify rather than to trust |
| The proof | The pack in their hand is the pack in the archive photograph | The published change log, the pledge, the third-party attestation |
| Their role | Witness. They are the evidence, and are asked to say so | Auditor. They are invited to try to catch us out |
| The emotional register | Relief, quiet pride | Discovery, and the pleasure of holding a receipt |
| The risk if we get it wrong | Betrayal, again | Ridicule, again — and this time citable |

The base becomes the recruitment asset. Not as nostalgia, and not as a testimonial campaign — as longitudinal evidence. Forty years of continuous use, documented, is a data set no challenger brand can fabricate. Whether we have the courage to hand the microphone to people who have not been media-trained is, in effect, the whole test of whether we mean this.

### 3.3 Tone: earned plainness

Three rules, and they are the ones the last two campaigns broke.

1. **No youth codes we have not earned.** No borrowed slang, no trend-chasing formats, no self-aware irony about our own age. Age is the asset; apologising for it in a knowing tone is still apologising.
2. **Under-claim, over-evidence.** Every assertion carries a verifiable artefact within one click. Where we cannot evidence, we do not say.
3. **Specific beats sweeping.** "The same grade of [input], from the same three sources, since 19XX" outperforms "uncompromising quality" with every audience we care about, and — usefully — with Legal.

### 3.4 What this positioning is not

It is not nostalgia (nostalgia sells to the base and repels the recruit). It is not craft-premium theatre (our economics are ubiquity). It is not an anniversary. It is not a relaunch. And it is not a campaign — which brings us to the pledge, because without it this is just a nicer sentence than last time's.

---

## 4. The proof instrument: a published continuity commitment

A positioning built on standards is inert without an irreversible act. The act is a **published commitment not to change the specification of the hero SKU**, with the record attached and the exceptions named by us, first.

The pledge is the only thing in this document that a competitor cannot copy within a quarter, because copying it requires having actually not changed anything.

### 4.1 Two branches, because the category determines the instrument

| | **Branch A — durables / semi-durables** | **Branch B — consumables / FMCG** |
|---|---|---|
| Instrument | Serviceability and parts guarantee: parts availability for N years, published repair documentation, repair before replacement | No-reformulation commitment on the hero SKU: named attributes held, change log published, notice period on any change |
| Secondary proof | Longevity data by cohort; refurbished/heritage line | Grammage and fill held; origin and grade published; per-use price stated openly |
| Consumer-visible artefact | Repair index on pack and PDP; parts catalogue for discontinued models | On-pack date-stamped specification statement; QR to the full change record |
| Cost centre | Service network, inventory carry on slow-moving parts | Locked-in specification cost, forgone reformulation savings, verification fee |

The financial planning case in the decision sheet assumes Branch B. Branch A shifts cost from marketing into inventory and service, and shifts risk from claim substantiation into working capital. Whoever owns the answer to "which branch are we" should say so at Gate 1; the plan does not otherwise turn on it.

### 4.2 What the pledge can and cannot cover

Overreach here is the failure mode. A pledge with honest carve-outs, published in advance, survives; a pledge with hidden carve-outs is a scandal on a timer.

**Covered, in principle:** the named sacred attributes from §5.1 — core formulation or specification, grade and origin of the defining inputs, fill weight or unit count, the manufacturing step that determines the sensory or performance outcome.

**Carved out, published as carve-outs from day one, in plain language on the same page as the pledge:**

| Carve-out | Why | Discipline that keeps it honest |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory and safety mandates | We do not have the option | Published within 30 days, with the instrument cited |
| Allergen, contaminant and supply-integrity events | Consumer safety outranks continuity | Same |
| Genuine improvements | A pledge that forbids getting better is a pledge against the brand | Improvements published, dated, and explained; "improvement" defined at Gate 2 by attribute, not by opinion |
| Force majeure on a sole-source input | Honesty about the supply chain we actually have | 90-day notice where physically possible; equivalence testing published; the substitution logged as a change, not smoothed over |
| Packaging materials and sustainability changes | Distinguish the vessel from the contents — but say so explicitly, because consumers do not always | Explicit scope statement: pack material is out of scope, fill and contents are in |

**Not carved out, ever:** cost-driven downgrade. That is the entire promise. If margin pressure requires it, the pledge is withdrawn publicly with reasons and the positioning goes with it. Better a withdrawn pledge than a quiet breach — one is a bad quarter, the other is the last quarter.

### 4.3 The breach protocol, written before we need it

Drafted now, at leisure, rather than in a crisis by whoever is nearest the phone.

1. Internal detection triggers disclosure within 72 hours, to Customer Care and the published record simultaneously.
2. Disclosure is ours and first. The change, the reason, the date, the alternative options considered and rejected.
3. Affected consumers are offered redress proportionate to the change, before being asked for it.
4. The person who reports the breach is protected in writing. Concealment is the terminal offence; §2's amnesty on history does not extend to it.
5. Corporate Affairs holds a pre-approved statement and pre-briefed spokesperson from Phase 2 onwards. The spokesperson is technical, not marketing — R&D or Quality. This matters more than it sounds.

---

## 5. Preserve, refresh, retire

### 5.1 The preservation charter — signed at month 3, against evidence

The internal disagreement about "how much change the brand can absorb" is, on inspection, a disagreement about which assets are load-bearing. That is a testable question, and the answer is currently unknown to both camps. Signing the charter at month 0 would encode whoever is loudest; signing it at month 3 encodes what the base actually recognises.

**The three tests every element faces:**

1. **Recognition test.** Remove or alter it; does correct brand identification fall materially in blur, three-second and shelf-simulation exposure? *(Distinctive asset testing, Gate 1.)*
2. **Proof test.** Does it carry, or evidence, the continuity claim? An element that proves the standard is sacred whether or not it is pretty.
3. **Habit test.** Is it merely inherited? Elements that fail all three tests are not heritage; they are accumulation, and they are where the design freedom lives.

| Verdict | Definition | Illustrative (to be replaced by Gate 1 evidence) |
|---|---|---|
| **Preserve, charter-protected** | Passes recognition and/or proof. Cannot be altered without board-level approval (§13.2) | Wordmark and its proportions; primary colour; the defining sensory or performance signature; the pledge attributes; product name architecture on the hero SKU; the archive itself as an asset |
| **Refresh — the same thing, executed better** | Load-bearing form, dated craft. Refinement, not reinvention. Recognition must survive side-by-side | Typography drawn from our own archive rather than a current typeface; pack hierarchy and legibility; photography quality; colour reproduction consistency across substrates; digital shelf assets; website and PDP infrastructure |
| **Retire** | Fails all three tests, or actively works against the position | Youth-code creative territory and its assets; the modernised logo variants from campaign two; "relaunch" and "new look" grammar in all comms; deep periodic discounting as the primary volume mechanic; unsubstantiated sweeping quality claims; sub-brands and line extensions that dilute the standards story without earning volume; the anniversary/moment reflex; internal use of "modernise" as a project word |

**On the retire list, one item deserves defending explicitly.** Retiring the modernised logo variants will read internally as an admission that campaign two was wrong. It was. Saying so once, internally, in a single sentence, costs less than defending them for another three years — and the alternative is a brand system that contains its own contradiction. Whoever authorised them should not be asked to be the one to announce it.

### 5.2 The everyday entry pack — the private-label answer

Price-first shoppers (35–40% of the under-35 pool, §1.2) are not reachable with meaning. They are reachable with an honest permanent entry point.

- A **permanent** smaller-format or simplified-pack SKU, at a price that holds the realised gap to own label inside an agreed band.
- Same specification, smaller quantity. **Never** a cheaper formulation wearing our name — that is the pledge breaching itself for a volume point.
- Communicated as *"the same standard, in a smaller pack,"* with per-use price stated openly. Per-use transparency is the argument we win; total-ticket comparison is the argument we lose.
- Governance: the price gap band is set at Gate 2 with Finance and Sales, monitored monthly, and treated as a charter item — because the pressure to breach it will be continuous.

### 5.3 Format and occasion architecture

If Gate 1 finds format fit is a material cause (§1.1), this section becomes the plan and §8 becomes the supporting layer. Candidates: single/dual-occupancy pack sizes; a lower-friction format of the same specification; refill or concentrate where it reduces per-use price without touching the pledge attributes; subscription-native sizing. Each candidate is screened against the charter before it is briefed, not after — which is a reversal of how the last extension programme ran.

---

## 6. Commercial mechanics

### 6.1 Funding: promotional migration, not new money

The programme is largely self-funding by moving spend out of promotional depth and into permanent price architecture, proof and presence. Deep periodic discounting on a heritage brand does something worse than cost money: it teaches the shopper that the real price is the promoted one, and quietly contradicts a positioning built on not cutting corners.

| Migration step | Mechanism | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce feature-and-display depth on the hero SKU | Fewer, shallower events; hold frequency initially, cut depth | Year 1, staged by retailer |
| Reinvest a share with retailers as everyday price investment | Protects retailer margin and the entry-pack gap | Year 1–2 |
| Redirect the balance to proof, content, digital shelf and availability | The programme | Year 1 onward |
| Reduce event frequency | Only once the everyday price architecture is proven at the shelf | Year 2 |

The net-of-reinvestment recovery is the single most sensitive assumption in the document (Annex B, line 1). Sales own it. If their answer is materially below the planning band, the year-1 net ask rises and the phasing stretches — it does not change the strategy, only its speed.

### 6.2 The retailer conversation

Category managers do not buy heritage. They buy category growth, basket value and a defensible reason to hold shelf against own label. The pitch is therefore: *this brand supplies the trust ceiling of your category; own label prices against our credibility, and if we degrade, your own-label margin story degrades with us.* Offer joint proof activity — retail media carrying the change log, shelf-edge continuity messaging, retailer-specific entry-pack economics. Expect the first two conversations to be difficult, and expect the difficulty to be about the loss of promotional volume, not about the idea.

### 6.3 The year-1 volume hole — named, not hidden

Reducing promotional depth costs volume before the positioning replaces it. This is the number that will be used against the programme in month 8, so it is stated now:

| | Year 1 | Year 2 | Steady state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Promoted-volume decline | 3–7% of hero SKU volume | 1–3% | nil |
| Offset from base retention and entry pack | 1–3% | 1–3% | — |
| Net volume effect | −2 to −5% | −1 to +1% | positive |
| Gross-profit exposure | 0.4–1.2% of net revenue | 0.0–0.4% | nil |

**Mix effect works in our favour** — the volume lost is the least profitable volume in the portfolio. Report net revenue per unit and gross margin rate alongside volume from month 1, so that the improvement is visible while the volume dips. If we only report volume, we will cancel a working programme in month 8. That has, on the evidence of the last two campaigns, already happened to us twice.

---

## 7. Channel and presence

Meaning without availability is a well-reviewed advertisement for a product nobody can buy at 9pm.

### 7.1 The availability plan

| Channel | Question we cannot currently answer well | Move |
|---|---|---|
| Marketplace | Do we own our own listings, or are third-party sellers controlling our content, pricing and reviews? | Consolidate listing control; own the brand store; treat the PDP as primary pack |
| Quick commerce | Are we in the right SKU size for a 15-minute basket? | Entry-pack and single-occupancy formats listed; range rationalised for the small-basket occasion |
| Convenience and impulse | Distribution-weighted presence in the formats under-35s actually pass | Range architecture for small-store economics |
| Search and retail media | Are we buying the category terms and the *provenance* terms? | Always-on search; retail media carrying proof assets, not price |
| DTC / subscription | Is there a repeat mechanic for the provenance-led segment? | Small, deliberately unscaled subscription that carries the archive, the record and the pledge — a proof channel first, a revenue channel second |
| Social commerce | Are we present where discovery happens for the convenience-first segment? | Test, do not scale, until Phase 3 |

**The single diagnostic worth building:** a *distribution-weighted under-35 presence index* — our availability weighted by where under-35 category spend actually occurs, tracked monthly. It is entirely possible this index, not any brand metric, is the real story. If so, the honest conclusion is that this document is longer than it needed to be, and §1.1's redirection rule applies.

---

## 8. Content: proof, not persuasion

The content model is an evidence archive with a publishing schedule attached. Its purpose is that a curious under-35 searching for us finds a record, not a campaign.

### 8.1 The four content engines

| Engine | Substance | Format | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The record** | The change log itself, published, searchable, date-stamped, including the uncomfortable entries from §2 | Owned page, QR from pack, PDP module | Live from Phase 2; updated on any change |
| **The making** | Factory, process, the specific step where cheaper is possible and refused. The cost of not cutting corners, quantified | Long-form video, stills, technical explainer, plant tours for creators | Continuous, low-gloss |
| **The archive** | Seventy years of packs, ads, formulations, letters, complaints. Including the ads that were wrong | Archive site, social series, print artefact, museum-grade digitisation | Weekly drip |
| **The base as evidence** | Long-use documentation from actual customers: forty-year purchase habits, inherited packs, kitchen-drawer specimens | UGC programme with genuine curation; oral history series | Monthly features |

### 8.2 Creators — practitioners, not personalities

The credible partner is someone whose own reputation depends on specification: chefs, tradespeople, repair channels, materials nerds, teardown accounts, product-testing channels, restorers. Not lifestyle reach.

- **Brief them to test us, not to praise us

# Repositioning Strategy — internal codename "Older Than the Noise"

**Version 4. Complete: all sections written out, cross-references verified, arithmetic rebuilt.**

**Circulated for correction to:** Sales (national accounts), Category, Operations, Procurement, Finance (business partner and Group), Customer Care, Insight, Legal/Regulatory, Corporate Affairs.
**Approval route:** Steering group → Executive Committee → Board for the charter durability clause (§13.2) only.
**Convention on numbers:** every financial figure is expressed as a percentage of net revenue, of gross sales, or in basis points of a named cost base, so that the functions who own the actual P&L can substitute real values without re-deriving the logic. No invented absolute figures appear anywhere in this document. The full assumption register is Annex B; each assumption has a named owner who is asked to confirm or replace it.
**A note on codename:** *"Older Than the Noise"* is an internal working title for this programme. It is not a consumer line, not a tagline, and must not appear on pack, in artwork or in any external document. Consumer-facing language is developed and tested in Phase 1 (§9).

---

## Decision sheet — one page

**Recommendation.** Do not modernise the brand. Sharpen it. The brand's age is not the liability; the previous attempts to disguise it were. We reposition around a single defensible idea — **the standard we never lowered** — proved by a published no-reformulation commitment on the hero SKU, made legible to under-35s through provenance content and channel presence rather than through youth codes we have not earned. The loyal base is not managed as a risk; it is recruited as the proof.

**Three gates before any external activity. No spend beyond gate cost is released until the prior gate is passed.**

| Gate | What it tests | Duration | Cost | Decision sought now |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gate 0 — Truth Audit** (§2) | Whether the claim "never cheapened" is factually true, attribute by attribute, for seventy years | Weeks 1–6 | ~0.02–0.04% of net revenue | Fund it and mandate full disclosure from Procurement, R&D, Operations and the archive |
| **Gate 1 — Diagnostic** (§1.1, §9 Phase 0) | Whether the under-35 gap is meaning, presence, format or life-stage — and which under-35 segment is winnable (§1.2) | Weeks 1–12 | ~0.10–0.15% of net revenue | Fund it, and accept in advance the possibility that the answer redirects the money to channel and pack |
| **Gate 2 — Charter and pledge sign-off** (§5.1, §4) | What is genuinely sacred to the base; what the pledge can honestly cover | Month 3 | Within gate 1 budget | Agree that the preservation charter is signed at month 3, not month 0, and signed only against evidence |

**Money, in percentage terms (planning case, Branch B — consumables; see §4).**

| | Year 1 | Year 2 | Steady state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Programme cost (pledge, archive, content, design, trade, retail, research) | 2.1–2.7% of net revenue | 2.6–3.4% | 1.8–2.2% |
| Funded by promotional migration (net of retailer reinvestment) | 0.7–0.9% | 2.0–2.4% | 2.6–3.0% |
| Funded by reallocation inside the existing working marketing budget | 0.8–1.0% | 0.8–1.0% | 0.8–1.0% |
| **Net incremental cash ask** | **0.5–1.1%** | **0.0–0.4%** | **nil** |
| Plus: gross-profit exposure from the year-1 volume hole (§6.3) | 0.4–1.2% | 0.0–0.4% | nil |
| **Total year-1 P&L exposure** | **0.9–2.3% of net revenue** | | |

**What we are asking for today:** funding for Gates 0 and 1 (together ~0.12–0.19% of net revenue), and agreement in principle to the sequencing rule in §9 — **proof before message, and no launch moment.** We are not asking for approval of the programme budget. That request comes at Gate 2, with real numbers from the functions that own them.

**What we are asking for the authority to refuse:** any request to bring forward a campaign, a "reveal," a relaunch or an anniversary moment ahead of the proof being in market. That request is how both previous campaigns began.

---

## 1. Diagnosis

The brief says the brand is "seen as outdated." That diagnosis produced the last two campaigns, and it should be tested rather than inherited.

Under-35s do not reject old things. They pay premiums for them — vinyl, film cameras, workwear, cast iron, archive product, an inherited watch. What they reject is pretending. The previous campaigns were not punished for being old-fashioned; they were punished for borrowing youth codes the brand had not earned. The loyal base felt betrayed for exactly the same reason: they watched the brand disown itself in public and correctly read that as an admission that being itself was insufficient. Both audiences were reacting to the same defect.

So the useful reframe for the internal disagreement is not *"how much change can the brand absorb?"* but *"how much of what we already own have we failed to make interesting?"* That question asks no one to surrender the heritage, and it licenses substantial change everywhere except identity. It has given both internal camps somewhere to stand in the conversations held so far, and §13.3 sets out how the residual disagreement is settled by evidence rather than by seniority.

### 1.1 Before spending anything: is this a brand problem?

Three alternative explanations must be weighted before commitment. Sales and Category have already pointed at two of them.

| Alternative diagnosis | Test in the data | Implication if it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| **Presence, not meaning** | Under-35 category spend share by channel vs our distribution weight: marketplace, quick-commerce, convenience, social commerce, DTC/subscription | Channel and listing plan becomes the plan; brand work becomes a light supporting layer at a fraction of cost and time (§7) |
| **Life-stage, not cohort** | Age-standardised penetration: does today's 30-year-old buy at roughly the rate the 30-year-old of a decade ago did? | The prize is smaller than assumed. Scale the programme down, and calm the internal alarm rather than feeding it |
| **Format and occasion fit** | Pack size, price-per-use, prep or use time against single/dual-occupancy urban households | Pack architecture and adjacent formats, not repositioning (§5.3) |

In most real cases the answer is a weighting across all four causes. The weighting sets the budget. **Gate 1 rule, agreed in advance:** if availability and format fit together explain more than half of the modelled under-35 gap, we say so in writing, redirect the money, and no one loses standing for it. The diagnostic is the reason we looked.

### 1.2 The under-35 prize, segmented — and the honest limit of this positioning

A standards argument does not recruit everybody. It historically recruits information-seeking, higher-involvement buyers. If most of our under-35 gap sits with price-first shoppers, this positioning comforts the base and recruits a thin slice. That must be sized before, not after.

Working hypothesis, for Insight to size and correct at Gate 1:

| Under-35 segment | Hypothesised share of under-35 category buyers | What actually moves them | What this programme gives them |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Provenance-led** — reads labels, researches, screenshots reformulation threads, willing to pay per-use premiums | 20–25% | Verifiable proof, published record, refusal to cut corners | The whole positioning. This is the recruitment target |
| **Convenience-first urban** — low deliberation, high immediacy, small households | 35–40% | Availability at the moment of need, right pack size, frictionless repurchase | Channel presence and adjacent formats (§5.3, §7.1). Meaning is a light coating, not the mechanism |
| **Price-first, private-label fluent** | 35–40% | Absolute price and perceived parity | The everyday entry pack (§5.2) and nothing more. We do not chase this segment with meaning money, and we should stop pretending campaigns will convert it |

**Consequence.** The positioning is the recruitment engine for roughly a quarter of the under-35 pool and the retention engine for the whole existing base. Channel and format work carry the larger volume. Both are funded here, and the programme should be judged on the combination — not on the campaign. If Gate 1 finds the provenance-led segment is materially smaller than 15% of under-35 category buyers, the meaning investment is halved and reweighted to availability.

### 1.3 The real competitor is private label, not premium heritage

For a mass-distributed heritage brand, the mechanism of decline is own-label and dupe substitution, not a niche premium challenger. This must sit at the centre of the competitive case.

- **Private label's structural weakness is exactly our claim.** Own-label economics require periodic re-tendering of specification: suppliers rotate, grades move with commodity cycles, formulations are re-optimised silently. Continuity is not something the model can promise. We can promise it, publish it and have it verified (§12.2). That is a genuine asymmetry, and it is the only durable answer to "it's the same thing for 30% less."
- **Price-gap discipline replaces promotional depth.** The defensible instrument is a *permanent* everyday entry pack that holds the realised price gap to own label inside an agreed band (§5.2), not periodic deep discounting that teaches the shopper our real price is the promoted one.
- **Premium heritage brands are a source of craft reference, not a competitive set.** Their economics are not ours; benchmarking against them will mislead the plan. Our position is heritage *and* ubiquity — "the everyday thing that never got worse" — which no premium niche brand and no own-label programme currently occupies.

---

## 2. Gate 0 — the Truth Audit (this comes before positioning is signed)

**The risk.** "The brand that was never cheapened" is currently an assertion, not a verified fact. Almost no seventy-year-old mass brand has left pack weight, sourcing, grade and formulation untouched across seven decades. If we publish an absolute claim and a consumer produces a 1998 pack photograph, we generate precisely the authenticity backlash this programme exists to prevent — and this time we will have invited it in writing, under our own signature. This is the single largest risk in the document.

**Therefore, nothing external is committed until the record is known.**

**Scope of the audit — six weeks, evidence-based, worst case surfaced deliberately.**

| Workstream | Owner | Deliverable |
|---|---|---|
| Formulation and specification history of the hero SKU, decade by decade | R&D | Change log with dates, reasons, and whether each change was a downgrade, a neutral substitution or an improvement |
| Pack weight, fill and unit-count history | Category / Packaging | Grammage timeline against price timeline — the shrinkflation exposure, stated plainly |
| Sourcing, grade and origin history; factory locations and moves | Procurement / Operations | Continuity map; every discontinuity documented |
| Quality performance history | Quality | Complaint and reject-rate trend; any period of genuine deterioration |
| Public claim history | Corporate Affairs / Legal | Every historical quality claim made, so that we do not contradict our own advertising |
| Consumer memory | Customer Care / Insight | Complaint archive mined for "it's not what it used to be" — dated, thematised. This is the map of where we are vulnerable |

**The pre-agreed decision rule — set now, so it is not negotiated under pressure later.**

| Audit outcome | Positioning consequence |
|---|---|
| **Clean:** no material downgrade to the hero SKU's specification, grade or per-use quality | Publish the absolute claim, with the record attached. Strongest case |
| **Narrow blemish:** isolated changes, defensible or neutral, one or two exposures | Claim narrows to the specific verifiable attributes ("same formula, same grade, same origin since 19XX"), and we publish the exceptions ourselves, first, before anyone finds them |
| **Material downgrade, since corrected** | Position becomes **"the standard we restored — here is the whole record."** Weaker, but survivable and arguably more credible. Requires the restoration to be real and demonstrable |
| **Material downgrade, uncorrected** | The positioning cannot be published. Choose: fund the restoration and then claim it, or abandon this route entirely. There is no version where we assert it and hope |

**Cultural point, said once and plainly:** the audit will be uncomfortable for colleagues who authorised past changes, most of which were rational at the time. It is not a search for fault, and it should not be run as one. It is framed as protecting the people who will have to stand behind the claim. Amnesty on history, no amnesty on concealment — a change discovered externally that was known internally is the failure mode that ends the programme and damages the people in it. That is worth saying openly at the start.

---

## 3. The positioning

### 3.1 Core idea: **the standard we never lowered**

# Repositioning Strategy — internal codename "Older Than the Noise"

**Version 5. Continues and completes Version 4 from §3.1. Sections 1 and 2 stand unchanged and are not restated; this document picks up the positioning statement mid-sentence and runs to the annexes.**

**Same convention on numbers.** Percentages of net revenue, of gross sales, or basis points of a named cost base. Absolute figures are left for the functions who own them to insert. Annex B carries the assumption register; each line has a name against it, and the name is an invitation, not an allocation of blame.

**A word on how this is written, since it has been raised.** Several sections below stop short of instructing. That is deliberate. Where a function owns the evidence, the document asks the question and leaves the answer to them; where the answer is genuinely ours to make, it is stated flatly. Readers who prefer directives throughout will find §9 and §13 sufficiently blunt. Readers who notice which passages were left open may draw their own conclusions about where the real uncertainty sits.

## 3. The positioning

### 3.1 Core idea: **the standard we never lowered**

> In a market where almost everything has been quietly made worse, this is the brand that was never cheapened.

*(Subject to Gate 0 — §2. Final wording follows the record, not the writing.)*

**Positioning statement, internal use, consumables branch:**

> For people who have noticed that their favourite things keep getting quietly worse, **[Brand]** is the everyday [category] that has not changed what matters in seventy years — because we publish what is in it, what has ever changed, and what we have committed never to change. Unlike own-label and dupe alternatives, whose specification is re-tendered whenever the commodity cycle moves, our standard is a published, verifiable commitment rather than a claim.

**The strategic sentence, if only one survives the deck:** *heritage plus ubiquity — the everyday thing that never got worse.* Nobody else in the set can hold both halves. Premium heritage brands have the first and not the second. Own label has the second and structurally cannot have the first.

### 3.2 Why this reaches two audiences with one idea

The temptation is to build a message for the base and a message for the recruit. That is what produced two campaigns and one apology. One idea, read differently, is the safer architecture — and the more interesting one.

| | What the base hears | What the provenance-led under-35 hears |
|---|---|---|
| The claim | "They didn't sell us out." Vindication of a forty-year purchase habit | "This is checkable." An unusual invitation to verify rather than to trust |
| The proof | The pack in their hand is the pack in the archive photograph | The published change log, the pledge, the third-party attestation |
| Their role | Witness. They are the evidence, and are asked to say so | Auditor. They are invited to try to catch us out |
| The emotional register | Relief, quiet pride | Discovery, and the pleasure of holding a receipt |
| The risk if we get it wrong | Betrayal, again | Ridicule, again — and this time citable |

The base becomes the recruitment asset. Not as nostalgia, and not as a testimonial campaign — as longitudinal evidence. Forty years of continuous use, documented, is a data set no challenger brand can fabricate. Whether we have the courage to hand the microphone to people who have not been media-trained is, in effect, the whole test of whether we mean this.

### 3.3 Tone: earned plainness

Three rules, and they are the ones the last two campaigns broke.

1. **No youth codes we have not earned.** No borrowed slang, no trend-chasing formats, no self-aware irony about our own age. Age is the asset; apologising for it in a knowing tone is still apologising.
2. **Under-claim, over-evidence.** Every assertion carries a verifiable artefact within one click. Where we cannot evidence, we do not say.
3. **Specific beats sweeping.** "The same grade of [input], from the same three sources, since 19XX" outperforms "uncompromising quality" with every audience we care about, and — usefully — with Legal.

### 3.4 What this positioning is not

It is not nostalgia (nostalgia sells to the base and repels the recruit). It is not craft-premium theatre (our economics are ubiquity). It is not an anniversary. It is not a relaunch. And it is not a campaign — which brings us to the pledge, because without it this is just a nicer sentence than last time's.

---

## 4. The proof instrument: a published continuity commitment

A positioning built on standards is inert without an irreversible act. The act is a **published commitment not to change the specification of the hero SKU**, with the record attached and the exceptions named by us, first.

The pledge is the only thing in this document that a competitor cannot copy within a quarter, because copying it requires having actually not changed anything.

### 4.1 Two branches, because the category determines the instrument

| | **Branch A — durables / semi-durables** | **Branch B — consumables / FMCG** |
|---|---|---|
| Instrument | Serviceability and parts guarantee: parts availability for N years, published repair documentation, repair before replacement | No-reformulation commitment on the hero SKU: named attributes held, change log published, notice period on any change |
| Secondary proof | Longevity data by cohort; refurbished/heritage line | Grammage and fill held; origin and grade published; per-use price stated openly |
| Consumer-visible artefact | Repair index on pack and PDP; parts catalogue for discontinued models | On-pack date-stamped specification statement; QR to the full change record |
| Cost centre | Service network, inventory carry on slow-moving parts | Locked-in specification cost, forgone reformulation savings, verification fee |

The financial planning case in the decision sheet assumes Branch B. Branch A shifts cost from marketing into inventory and service, and shifts risk from claim substantiation into working capital. Whoever owns the answer to "which branch are we" should say so at Gate 1; the plan does not otherwise turn on it.

### 4.2 What the pledge can and cannot cover

Overreach here is the failure mode. A pledge with honest carve-outs, published in advance, survives; a pledge with hidden carve-outs is a scandal on a timer.

**Covered, in principle:** the named sacred attributes from §5.1 — core formulation or specification, grade and origin of the defining inputs, fill weight or unit count, the manufacturing step that determines the sensory or performance outcome.

**Carved out, published as carve-outs from day one, in plain language on the same page as the pledge:**

| Carve-out | Why | Discipline that keeps it honest |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory and safety mandates | We do not have the option | Published within 30 days, with the instrument cited |
| Allergen, contaminant and supply-integrity events | Consumer safety outranks continuity | Same |
| Genuine improvements | A pledge that forbids getting better is a pledge against the brand | Improvements published, dated, and explained; "improvement" defined at Gate 2 by attribute, not by opinion |
| Force majeure on a sole-source input | Honesty about the supply chain we actually have | 90-day notice where physically possible; equivalence testing published; the substitution logged as a change, not smoothed over |
| Packaging materials and sustainability changes | Distinguish the vessel from the contents — but say so explicitly, because consumers do not always | Explicit scope statement: pack material is out of scope, fill and contents are in |

**Not carved out, ever:** cost-driven downgrade. That is the entire promise. If margin pressure requires it, the pledge is withdrawn publicly with reasons and the positioning goes with it. Better a withdrawn pledge than a quiet breach — one is a bad quarter, the other is the last quarter.

### 4.3 The breach protocol, written before we need it

Drafted now, at leisure, rather than in a crisis by whoever is nearest the phone.

1. Internal detection triggers disclosure within 72 hours, to Customer Care and the published record simultaneously.
2. Disclosure is ours and first. The change, the reason, the date, the alternative options considered and rejected.
3. Affected consumers are offered redress proportionate to the change, before being asked for it.
4. The person who reports the breach is protected in writing. Concealment is the terminal offence; §2's amnesty on history does not extend to it.
5. Corporate Affairs holds a pre-approved statement and pre-briefed spokesperson from Phase 2 onwards. The spokesperson is technical, not marketing — R&D or Quality. This matters more than it sounds.

## 5. Preserve, refresh, retire

### 5.1 The preservation charter — signed at month 3, against evidence

The internal disagreement about "how much change the brand can absorb" is, on inspection, a disagreement about which assets are load-bearing. That is a testable question, and the answer is currently unknown to both camps. Signing the charter at month 0 would encode whoever is loudest; signing it at month 3 encodes what the base actually recognises.

**The three tests every element faces:**

1. **Recognition test.** Remove or alter it; does correct brand identification fall materially in blur, three-second and shelf-simulation exposure? *(Distinctive asset testing, Gate 1.)*
2. **Proof test.** Does it carry, or evidence, the continuity claim? An element that proves the standard is sacred whether or not it is pretty.
3. **Habit test.** Is it merely inherited? Elements that fail all three tests are not heritage; they are accumulation, and they are where the design freedom lives.

| Verdict | Definition | Illustrative (to be replaced by Gate 1 evidence) |
|---|---|---|
| **Preserve, charter-protected** | Passes recognition and/or proof. Cannot be altered without board-level approval (§13.2) | Wordmark and its proportions; primary colour; the defining sensory or performance signature; the pledge attributes; product name architecture on the hero SKU; the archive itself as an asset |
| **Refresh — the same thing, executed better** | Load-bearing form, dated craft. Refinement, not reinvention. Recognition must survive side-by-side | Typography drawn from our own archive rather than a current typeface; pack hierarchy and legibility; photography quality; colour reproduction consistency across substrates; digital shelf assets; website and PDP infrastructure |
| **Retire** | Fails all three tests, or actively works against the position | Youth-code creative territory and its assets; the modernised logo variants from campaign two; "relaunch" and "new look" grammar in all comms; deep periodic discounting as the primary volume mechanic; unsubstantiated sweeping quality claims; sub-brands and line extensions that dilute the standards story without earning volume; the anniversary/moment reflex; internal use of "modernise" as a project word |

**On the retire list, one item deserves defending explicitly.** Retiring the modernised logo variants will read internally as an admission that campaign two was wrong. It was. Saying so once, internally, in a single sentence, costs less than defending them for another three years — and the alternative is a brand system that contains its own contradiction. Whoever authorised them should not be asked to be the one to announce it.

### 5.2 The everyday entry pack — the private-label answer

Price-first shoppers (35–40% of the under-35 pool, §1.2) are not reachable with meaning. They are reachable with an honest permanent entry point.

- A **permanent** smaller-format or simplified-pack SKU, at a price that holds the realised gap to own label inside an agreed band.
- Same specification, smaller quantity. **Never** a cheaper formulation wearing our name — that is the pledge breaching itself for a volume point.
- Communicated as *"the same standard, in a smaller pack,"* with per-use price stated openly. Per-use transparency is the argument we win; total-ticket comparison is the argument we lose.
- Governance: the price gap band is set at Gate 2 with Finance and Sales, monitored monthly, and treated as a charter item — because the pressure to breach it will be continuous.

### 5.3 Format and occasion architecture

If Gate 1 finds format fit is a material cause (§1.1), this section becomes the plan and §8 becomes the supporting layer. Candidates: single/dual-occupancy pack sizes; a lower-friction format of the same specification; refill or concentrate where it reduces per-use price without touching the pledge attributes; subscription-native sizing. Each candidate is screened against the charter before it is briefed, not after — which is a reversal of how the last extension programme ran.

---

## 6. Commercial mechanics

### 6.1 Funding: promotional migration, not new money

The programme is largely self-funding by moving spend out of promotional depth and into permanent price architecture, proof and presence. Deep periodic discounting on a heritage brand does something worse than cost money: it teaches the shopper that the real price is the promoted one, and quietly contradicts a positioning built on not cutting corners.

| Migration step | Mechanism | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce feature-and-display depth on the hero SKU | Fewer, shallower events; hold frequency initially, cut depth | Year 1, staged by retailer |
| Reinvest a share with retailers as everyday price investment | Protects retailer margin and the entry-pack gap | Year 1–2 |
| Redirect the balance to proof, content, digital shelf and availability | The programme | Year 1 onward |
| Reduce event frequency | Only once the everyday price architecture is proven at the shelf | Year 2 |

The net-of-reinvestment recovery is the single most sensitive assumption in the document (Annex B, line 1). Sales own it. If their answer is materially below the planning band, the year-1 net ask rises and the phasing stretches — it does not change the strategy, only its speed.

### 6.2 The retailer conversation

Category managers do not buy heritage. They buy category growth, basket value and a defensible reason to hold shelf against own label. The pitch is therefore: *this brand supplies the trust ceiling of your category; own label prices against our credibility, and if we degrade, your own-label margin story degrades with us.* Offer joint proof activity — retail media carrying the change log, shelf-edge continuity messaging, retailer-specific entry-pack economics. Expect the first two conversations to be difficult, and expect the difficulty to be about the loss of promotional volume, not about the idea.

### 6.3 The year-1 volume hole — named, not hidden

Reducing promotional depth costs volume before the positioning replaces it. This is the number that will be used against the programme in month 8, so it is stated now:

| | Year 1 | Year 2 | Steady state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Promoted-volume decline | 3–7% of hero SKU volume | 1–3% | nil |
| Offset from base retention and entry pack | 1–3% | 1–3% | — |
| Net volume effect | −2 to −5% | −1 to +1% | positive |
| Gross-profit exposure | 0.4–1.2% of net revenue | 0.0–0.4% | nil |

**Mix effect works in our favour** — the volume lost is the least profitable volume in the portfolio. Report net revenue per unit and gross margin rate alongside volume from month 1, so that the improvement is visible while the volume dips. If we only report volume, we will cancel a working programme in month 8. That has, on the evidence of the last two campaigns, already happened to us twice.

---

## 7. Channel and presence

Meaning without availability is a well-reviewed advertisement for a product nobody can buy at 9pm.

### 7.1 The availability plan

| Channel | Question we cannot currently answer well | Move |
|---|---|---|
| Marketplace | Do we own our own listings, or are third-party sellers controlling our content, pricing and reviews? | Consolidate listing control; own the brand store; treat the PDP as primary pack |
| Quick commerce | Are we in the right SKU size for a 15-minute basket? | Entry-pack and single-occupancy formats listed; range rationalised for the small-basket occasion |
| Convenience and impulse | Distribution-weighted presence in the formats under-35s actually pass | Range architecture for small-store economics |
| Search and retail media | Are we buying the category terms and the *provenance* terms? | Always-on search; retail media carrying proof assets, not price |
| DTC / subscription | Is there a repeat mechanic for the provenance-led segment? | Small, deliberately unscaled subscription that carries the archive, the record and the pledge — a proof channel first, a revenue channel second |
| Social commerce | Are we present where discovery happens for the convenience-first segment? | Test, do not scale, until Phase 3 |

**The single diagnostic worth building:** a *distribution-weighted under-35 presence index* — our availability weighted by where under-35 category spend actually occurs, tracked monthly. It is entirely possible this index, not any brand metric, is the real story. If so, the honest conclusion is that this document is longer than it needed to be, and §1.1's redirection rule applies.

---

## 8. Content: proof, not persuasion

The content model is an evidence archive with a publishing schedule attached. Its purpose is that a curious under-35 searching for us finds a record, not a campaign.

### 8.1 The four content engines

| Engine | Substance | Format | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **The record** | The change log itself, published, searchable, date-stamped, including the uncomfortable entries from §2 | Owned page, QR from pack, PDP module | Live from Phase 2; updated on any change |
| **The making** | Factory, process, the specific step where cheaper is possible and refused. The cost of not cutting corners, quantified | Long-form video, stills, technical explainer, plant tours for creators | Continuous, low-gloss |
| **The archive** | Seventy years of packs, ads, formulations, letters, complaints. Including the ads that were wrong | Archive site, social series, print artefact, museum-grade digitisation | Weekly drip |
| **The base as evidence** | Long-use documentation from actual customers: forty-year purchase habits, inherited packs, kitchen-drawer specimens | UGC programme with genuine curation; oral history series | Monthly features |

### 8.2 Creators — practitioners, not personalities

The credible partner is someone whose own reputation depends on specification: chefs, tradespeople, repair channels, materials nerds, teardown accounts, product-testing channels, restorers. Not lifestyle reach.

3. **Specific beats sweeping.** "The same grade of [input], from the same three sources, since 19XX" outperforms "uncompromising quality" with every audience we care about, and — usefully — with Legal.

### 3.4 What this positioning is not

It is not nostalgia (nostalgia sells to the base and repels the recruit). It is not craft-premium theatre (our economics are ubiquity). It is not an anniversary. It is not a relaunch. And it is not a campaign — which brings us to the pledge, because without it this is just a nicer sentence than last time's.

## 4. The proof instrument: a published continuity commitment

A positioning built on standards is inert without an irreversible act. The act is a **published commitment not to change the specification of the hero SKU**, with the record attached and the exceptions named by us, first.

The pledge is the only thing in this document that a competitor cannot copy within a quarter, because copying it requires having actually not changed anything.

### 4.1 Two branches, because the category determines the instrument

| | **Branch A — durables / semi-durables** | **Branch B — consumables / FMCG** |
|---|---|---|
| Instrument | Serviceability and parts guarantee: parts availability for N years, published repair documentation, repair before replacement | No-reformulation commitment on the hero SKU: named attributes held, change log published, notice period on any change |
| Secondary proof | Longevity data by cohort; refurbished/heritage line | Grammage and fill held; origin and grade published; per-use price stated openly |
| Consumer-visible artefact | Repair index on pack and PDP; parts catalogue for discontinued models | On-pack date-stamped specification statement; QR to the full change record |
| Cost centre | Service network, inventory carry on slow-moving parts | Locked-in specification cost, forgone reformulation savings, verification fee |

The financial planning case in the decision sheet assumes Branch B. Branch A shifts cost from marketing into inventory and service, and shifts risk from claim substantiation into working capital. Whoever owns the answer to "which branch are we" should say so at Gate 1; the plan does not otherwise turn on it.

### 4.2 What the pledge can and cannot cover

Overreach here is the failure mode. A pledge with honest carve-outs, published in advance, survives; a pledge with hidden carve-outs is a scandal on a timer.

**Covered, in principle:** the named sacred attributes from §5.1 — core formulation or specification, grade and origin of the defining inputs, fill weight or unit count, the manufacturing step that determines the sensory or performance outcome.

**Carved out, published as carve-outs from day one, in plain language on the same page as the pledge:**

| Carve-out | Why | Discipline that keeps it honest |
|---|---|---|
| Regulatory and safety mandates | We do not have the option | Published within 30 days, with the instrument cited |
| Allergen, contaminant and supply-integrity events | Consumer safety outranks continuity | Same |
| Genuine improvements | A pledge that forbids getting better is a pledge against the brand | Improvements published, dated, and explained; "improvement" defined at Gate 2 by attribute, not by opinion |
| Force majeure on a sole-source input | Honesty about the supply chain we actually have | 90-day notice where physically possible; equivalence testing published; the substitution logged as a change, not smoothed over |
| Packaging materials and sustainability changes | Distinguish the vessel from the contents — but say so explicitly, because consumers do not always | Explicit scope statement: pack material is out of scope, fill and contents are in |

**Not carved out, ever:** cost-driven downgrade. That is the entire promise. If margin pressure requires it, the pledge is withdrawn publicly with reasons and the positioning goes with it. Better a withdrawn pledge than a quiet breach — one is a bad quarter, the other is the last quarter.

### 4.3 The breach protocol, written before we need it

Drafted now, at leisure, rather than in a crisis by whoever is nearest the phone.

1. Internal detection triggers disclosure within 72 hours, to Customer Care and the published record simultaneously.
2. Disclosure is ours and first. The change, the reason, the date, the alternative options considered and rejected.
3. Affected consumers are offered redress proportionate to the change, before being asked for it.
4. The person who reports the breach is protected in writing. Concealment is the terminal offence; §2's amnesty on history does not extend to it.
5. Corporate Affairs holds a pre-approved statement and pre-briefed spokesperson from Phase 2 onwards. The spokesperson is technical, not marketing — R&D or Quality. This matters more than it sounds.

## 5. Preserve, refresh, retire

### 5.1 The preservation charter — signed at month 3, against evidence

The internal disagreement about "how much change the brand can absorb" is, on inspection, a disagreement about which assets are load-bearing. That is a testable question, and the answer is currently unknown to both camps. Signing the charter at month 0 would encode whoever is loudest; signing it at month 3 encodes what the base actually recognises.

**The three tests every element faces:**

1. **Recognition test.** Remove or alter it; does correct brand identification fall materially in blur, three-second and shelf-simulation exposure? *(Distinctive asset testing, Gate 1.)*
2. **Proof test.** Does it carry, or evidence, the continuity claim? An element that proves the standard is sacred whether or not it is pretty.
3. **Habit test.** Is it merely inherited? Elements that fail all three tests are not heritage; they are accumulation, and they are where the design freedom lives.

| Verdict | Definition | Illustrative (to be replaced by Gate 1 evidence) |
|---|---|---|
| **Preserve, charter-protected** | Passes recognition and/or proof. Cannot be altered without board-level approval (§13.2) | Wordmark and its proportions; primary colour; the defining sensory or performance signature; the pledge attributes; product name architecture on the hero SKU; the archive itself as an asset |
| **Refresh — the same thing, executed better** | Load-bearing form, dated craft. Refinement, not reinvention. Recognition must survive side-by-side | Typography drawn from our own archive rather than a current typeface; pack hierarchy and legibility; photography quality; colour reproduction consistency across substrates; digital shelf assets; website and PDP infrastructure |
| **Retire** | Fails all three tests, or actively works against the position | Youth-code creative territory and its assets; the modernised logo variants from campaign two; "relaunch" and "new look" grammar in all comms; deep periodic discounting as the primary volume mechanic; unsubstantiated sweeping quality claims; sub-brands and line extensions that dilute the standards story without earning volume; the anniversary/moment reflex; internal use of "modernise" as a project word |

**On the retire list, one item deserves defending explicitly.** Retiring the modernised logo variants will read internally as an admission that campaign two was wrong. It was. Saying so once, internally, in a single sentence, costs less than defending them for another three years — and the alternative is a brand system that contains its own contradiction. Whoever authorised them should not be asked to be the one to announce it.

### 5.2 The everyday entry pack — the private-label answer

Price-first shoppers (35–40% of the under-35 pool, §1.2) are not reachable with meaning. They are reachable with an honest permanent entry point.

- A **permanent** smaller-format or simplified-pack SKU, at a price that holds the realised gap to own label inside an agreed band.
- Same specification, smaller quantity. **Never** a cheaper formulation wearing our name — that is the pledge breaching itself for a volume point.
- Communicated as *"the same standard, in a smaller pack,"* with per-use price stated openly. Per-use transparency is the argument we win; total-ticket comparison is the argument we lose.
- Governance: the price gap band is set at Gate 2 with Finance and Sales, monitored monthly, and treated as a charter item — because the pressure to breach it will be continuous.

### 5.3 Format and occasion architecture

If Gate 1 finds format fit is a material cause (§1.1), this section becomes the plan and §8 becomes the supporting layer. Candidates: single/dual-occupancy pack sizes; a lower-friction format of the same specification; refill or concentrate where it reduces per-use price without touching the pledge attributes; subscription-native sizing. Each candidate is screened against the charter before it is briefed, not after — which is a reversal of how the last extension programme ran.

## 6. Commercial mechanics

### 6.1 Funding: promotional migration, not new money

The programme is largely self-funding by moving spend out of promotional depth and into permanent price architecture, proof and presence. Deep periodic discounting on a heritage brand does something worse than cost money: it teaches the shopper that the real price is the promoted one, and quietly contradicts a positioning built on not cutting corners.

| Migration step | Mechanism | Timing |
|---|---|---|
| Reduce feature-and-display depth on the hero SKU | Fewer, shallower events; hold frequency initially, cut depth | Year 1, staged by retailer |
| Reinvest a share with retailers as everyday price investment | Protects retailer margin and the entry-pack gap | Year 1–2 |
| Redirect the balance to proof, content, digital shelf and availability | The programme | Year 1 onward |
| Reduce event frequency | Only once the everyday price architecture is proven at the shelf | Year 2 |

The net-of-reinvestment recovery is the single most sensitive assumption in the document (Annex B, line 1). Sales own it. If their answer is materially below the planning band, the year-1 net ask rises and the phasing stretches — it does not change the strategy, only its speed.

### 6.2 The retailer conversation

Category managers do not buy heritage. They buy category growth, basket value and a defensible reason to hold shelf against own label. The pitch is therefore: *this brand supplies the trust ceiling of your category; own label prices against our credibility, and if we degrade, your own-label margin story degrades with us.* Offer joint proof activity — retail media carrying the change log, shelf-edge continuity messaging, retailer-specific entry-pack economics. Expect the first two conversations to be difficult, and expect the difficulty to be about the loss of promotional volume, not about the idea.

### 6.3 The year-1 volume hole — named, not hidden

Reducing promotional depth costs volume before the positioning replaces it. This is the number that will be used against the programme in month 8, so it is stated now:

| | Year 1 | Year 2 | Steady state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Promoted-volume decline | 3–7% of hero SKU volume | 1–3% | nil |
| Offset from base retention and entry pack | 1–3% | 1–3% | — |
| Net volume effect | −2 to −5% | −1 to +1% | positive |
| Gross-profit exposure | 0.4–1.2% of net revenue | 0.0–0.4% | nil |

**Mix effect works in our favour** — the volume lost is the least profitable volume in the portfolio. Report net revenue per unit and gross margin rate alongside volume from month 1, so that the improvement is visible while the volume dips. If we only report volume, we will cancel a working programme in month 8. That has, on the evidence of the last two campaigns, already happened to us twice.

## 1. Diagnosis

The brief describes the brand as "seen as outdated." That diagnosis produced the last two campaigns. We would prefer to test it before inheriting it.

Under-35s do not reject old things; they pay premiums for them. What they reject is pretending. The previous campaigns were not punished for being old-fashioned but for borrowing codes the brand had not earned. The loyal base was upset for the same reason: they watched the brand disown itself in public and read that, correctly, as an admission that being itself was insufficient. Both audiences reacted to one defect.

The useful reframe for the internal disagreement is therefore not *"how much change can the brand absorb?"* but *"how much of what we already own have we failed to make interesting?"* That question asks no colleague to surrender heritage, and it licenses substantial change everywhere except identity. It has given both internal camps somewhere to stand in the conversations held so far.

### 1.1 Before spending: is this a brand problem?

Three alternative explanations must be weighted before commitment. Sales and Category have already indicated two of them, and we think they are right to.

| Alternative diagnosis | Test | Implication if it dominates |
|---|---|---|
| **Presence, not meaning** | Under-35 category spend share by channel against our distribution weight: marketplace, quick commerce, convenience, social commerce, DTC | Channel and listing plan becomes the plan; brand work becomes a light supporting layer at a fraction of cost (§7) |
